title: Trump Called Off Tuesday's Iran Strike. For India, the Real War Is Over Oil.
excerpt: A last-minute intervention by Gulf monarchies has paused what would have been the largest American military operation since 2003 — but for New Delhi and millions of Indians in the Gulf, the economic siege continues.
body:
On Monday evening, President Donald Trump revealed that a comprehensive American military strike on Iran — planned for Tuesday, May 19 — had been called off at the last moment. The leaders of Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates had personally asked him to hold fire, arguing that a new round of negotiations could end the three-month conflict without further bloodshed.

The cancellation averted what Pentagon officials described as a multi-wave, joint-force operation involving carrier-based aircraft, strategic bombers, and cruise missiles. Its objective was to break the strategic stalemate that has choked the Strait of Hormuz since April and sent oil markets into convulsions.

For India, the reprieve is welcome but insufficient. The world's third-largest oil importer has spent the past twelve weeks navigating a geopolitical obstacle course that threatens both its energy security and its vast diaspora in the Persian Gulf.

The Gulf's 8.5 Million Indians

The most immediate human stakes sit in the Gulf Cooperation Council states themselves. Roughly 8.5 million Indian nationals live and work across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, and Bahrain. They form the backbone of the construction, hospitality, healthcare, and technology sectors. In 2025, remittances from the Gulf to India exceeded $50 billion — a lifeline for families across Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Bihar.

A full-scale American bombardment of Iran would have triggered retaliatory strikes on Gulf infrastructure. Iran's military doctrine has long designated Western-aligned oil facilities, desalination plants, and commercial ports as legitimate counter-targets. The drone attack on the UAE's Barakah Nuclear Power Plant on May 17 — which struck an auxiliary generator just outside the reactor's security perimeter — offered a preview of the chaos that a wider war would unleash.

For the Indian workers whose livelihoods depend on Gulf economies functioning normally, every escalation carries the risk of mass displacement, frozen wages, and collapsed employment contracts. India's Ministry of External Affairs has quietly updated contingency evacuation plans, though officials have avoided public comment.

India's Oil Tightrope

Beyond the diaspora, the rupture in the Strait of Hormuz has forced India into an uncomfortable energy diplomacy. Before the conflict, roughly 60 percent of India's crude imports transited the strait. With that chokepoint effectively sealed by Iranian mines and fast-attack boats since mid-April, New Delhi has scrambled for alternatives.

The first lifeline has been Russian crude. India's imports from Russia hit record highs in April and early May, filling the gap left by the collapse of Middle Eastern supply. But the US sanctions waiver that permitted these purchases — General License 134B — expired on May 16. India has requested an extension, arguing that without Russian barrels, domestic fuel prices would spike further and the rupee's slide would accelerate. Washington has yet to respond.

The second front is Chabahar. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi used last week's BRICS gathering to urge India to continue developing the strategic port, which New Delhi views as its gateway to Central Asia and Afghanistan. But India's 2026-27 Union Budget conspicuously excluded Chabahar funding after the previous US sanctions waiver lapsed, leaving the $1.6 billion project in limbo.

Meanwhile, domestic voices are growing louder. A policy paper circulated among senior Commerce Ministry officials last week argued that India needs a dedicated law to shield its companies from extraterritorial US sanctions — a "blocking statute" similar to those enacted by the European Union. The proposal remains politically sensitive, given the broader India-US trade negotiations underway.

A Pause, Not a Peace

Trump's decision to stand down is explicitly temporary. He instructed Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman General Daniel Caine to maintain "hyper-readiness" and to be prepared to launch the full assault "on a moment's notice." The diplomatic window, brokered through Pakistani intermediaries, is measured in days, not weeks.

The sticking points are familiar: Washington demands that Iran permanently dismantle its enrichment programme and accept intrusive inspections; Tehran insists on the immediate lifting of all sanctions and the withdrawal of American naval forces from the Gulf. The gap between these positions remains vast.

For India's policymakers, the calculus is brutally simple. Every day the Hormuz crisis persists, the country's import bill swells, the rupee weakens, and the fiscal cushion provided by the RBI's record dividend to the government shrinks. Every day that Russian waivers remain uncertain, refiners face the prospect of operating without their primary replacement crude supply.

What It Means for the Diaspora

Indians abroad — whether in Dubai's financial towers, Doha's construction sites, or Houston's energy corridor — are watching this crisis through a lens that most Western commentary misses. The Gulf diaspora's economic wellbeing is directly tied to regional stability. NRIs with investments in Indian markets are calculating the damage of a rupee that has fallen more than seven percent since the conflict began. And families in India who depend on monthly transfers from the Gulf are quietly bracing for disruption.

Trump's pause buys time. It does not buy certainty. The next 72 hours will determine whether diplomacy can close the gap that three months of war have not — and whether India's delicate balancing act between Washington, Tehran, and Moscow can survive another escalation.

A full-scale US-Iran war would directly endanger their livelihoods, remittances home, and physical safety. Meanwhile, India's energy security hangs in the balance as it navigates sanctions on both Iranian and Russian crude.
